'''''Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] '''''Schlumbergera gaertneri''''' and '''''Hatiora gaertneri''''',<ref name=POWO_219239-2/> is a [[species]] of [[epiphyte|epiphytic]] cactus which belongs to the tribe [[Rhipsalideae]] within the subfamily [[Cactoideae]] of the [[Cactus|Cactaceae]]. Together with the hybrid with ''[[Rhipsalidopsis rosea|R. rosea]]'', '''''Rhipsalidopsis'' × ''graeseri''''', it is known, in English speaking countries in the Northern Hemisphere, as '''Easter cactus''' or '''Whitsun cactus''' and is a widely cultivated ornamental plant. It has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/33719/Hatiora-gaertneri/Details | title = ''Hatiora gaertneri'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 19 July 2020}}</ref>

==Description==

''Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri'' is found in southeastern [[Brazil]], in Paraná and Santa Catarina, at altitudes of {{convert|350|–|1300|m|ft|abbr=on|-2}}. ''R. gaertneri'' grows on trees ([[epiphyte|epiphytic]]) or less often rocks ([[lithophyte|lithophytic]]) in sub-tropical rain forest. With maturity, it develops into a branching pendant leafless shrub with a woody base. The stems are made up of segments, most of which are flattened and which are the [[photosynthesis|photosynthetic]] organs ([[cladode]]s) of the plant. Younger segments are dullish green, {{convert|4|–|7|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} long and {{convert|2|–|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide, with small notches on the margins. Structures characteristic of cacti, called [[areole]]s, form in these notches. Flowers form from areoles at the ends of the stems. These are scarlet in colour, {{convert|4|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} long, radially symmetrical (actinomorphic), opening to a funnel shape with a maximum diameter of about {{convert|4|–|7.5|cm|in|abbr=on|1}}. Red oblong [[fruit]]s form after the flowers are fertilized.<ref name=Ande2001a>{{Harvnb|Anderson|2001|pp=375–376}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
<!--There is a wikilink here from "Schlumbergera" so fix if you change the section title-->
Although cacti belonging to the tribe Rhipsalideae are quite distinct in appearance and habit from other cacti, as they grow on trees or rocks as epiphytes or lithophytes, for a long time there has been confusion as to how the species should be placed into genera. ''Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri'' was first described in 1884 by [[Eduard August von Regel|Eduard von Regel]] as the variety ''gaertneri'' of ''Epiphyllum russellianum'' (now ''[[Schlumbergera russelliana]]''). The name honours one of the Gaertner family, early settlers in [[Blumenau]], [[Brazil]].<ref>Eduard August von Regel. Gartenflora . volume  33. page323. 1884. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/42128303]</ref><ref>Arquivo Histórico José Ferreira da Silva. [http://arquivodeblumenau.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/1g.pdf]</ref>

The species has had a complex taxonomic history. In 1889, [[William Watson (19th century botanist)|William Watson]] elevated it to the full species ''Epiphyllum gaertneri'' and in 1913, [[Nathaniel Lord Britton|Nathaniel Britton]] and [[Joseph Nelson Rose|Josephy Rose]] transferred it to ''[[Schlumbergera]]'' as ''S. gaertneri''.<ref name=Ande2001a/> The relationship to ''S. russelliana'' was based on the appearance of the stems, made up of somewhat flattened segments with small teeth, and the radially symmetrical shape of the flowers. However, the deeper structure of the flower differs from ''Schlumbergera'' species, which have a short floral tube at the base of the flower formed by fused petals, and stamens arranged in two distinct series, whereas ''Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri'' has separate petals and a single series of stamens. ''Rh. gaertneri'' was separated from ''Schlumbergera'' as ''Rhipsalis gaertneri'' by [[Friedrich Karl Johann Vaupel|Friedrich Vaupel]] in 1925, after which it was successively transferred to ''Epiphyllopsis'' by [[Alwin Berger]] in 1929, ''Rhipsalidopsis'' by [[Karl Hermann Leonhard Lindinger]] in 1942, and ''Hatiora'' by [[Wilhelm A. Bathlott|Wilhelm Barthlott]] in 1987.<ref name=POWO_219239-2/><ref name=Ande2001a/> It was put back in ''Schlumbergera'' as the result of [[Molecular phylogenetics|molecular phylogenetic]] studies in 2011,<ref name=CalvZappForeLohm11/> and then restored to ''Rhipsalidopsis'' again.<ref name=POWO_219239-2/>

In horticultural sources, the Easter cactus continued to be referred to as ''Schlumbergera gaertneri'' (even when other sources placed it in ''Hatiora''),<ref name=IPC>{{Citation |title=Schlumbergera gaertneri – Easter cactus |website=indoor-plant-care.com |url=http://www.indoor-plant-care.com/plant-list/schlumbergera-gaertneri/ |access-date=2011-12-01 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613083808/http://www.indoor-plant-care.com/plant-list/schlumbergera-gaertneri/ |url-status=live |archivedate=2011-06-13 }}</ref> as well as ''Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri''.<ref name=Brun2001>{{Citation |last=Brunelle |first=Paul J. |year=2001 |title=Recognition and Culture of the Holiday Cacti |publisher=Dalhousie University |url=http://cactus.biology.dal.ca/paulS/christmas/christmas.html |access-date=2011-11-04 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20111107232711/http://cactus.biology.dal.ca/paulS/christmas/christmas.html |url-status=dead |archivedate=2011-11-07 }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Hatiora ×graeseri flower.jpg|thumb|Flower of ''Rhipsalidopsis'' × ''graeseri'' cultivar]]
[[File:Lidcactus 03.JPG|thumb|Flower of ''Rhipsalidopsis'' × ''graeseri'' cultivar]]
Under the name Easter cactus or Whitsun cactus, ''Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri'' is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant for its scarlet flowers. Its common names reflect the period in which it flowers in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], namely late Spring. It has been artificially{{explain|date=April 2024}} crossed with a pink-flowered species, ''[[Rhipsalidopsis rosea]]'', to form the hybrid ''Rhipsalidopsis'' × ''graeseri'', [[cultivar]]s of which have flowers in a wider range of colours.

The Easter cactus is considered more difficult to grow than the Christmas or Thanksgiving cactus (cultivars and hybrids of ''[[Schlumbergera]]'').<ref name=Brun2001/> Recommendations for care include:
* ''Temperature'' Summer temperatures around {{convert|25|°C|°F}} are suggested,<ref name=IPC/> with lower temperatures down to {{convert|7|–|13|°C|°F}} in the winter (November to January in the Northern Hemisphere) to initiate good bud formation.<ref name=Brun2001/>
* ''Light'' As epiphytic forest plants, they are not exposed to strong sunlight. Half-shade is recommended; plants can be placed outside in the summer.<ref name=Hech1997>{{Citation |last=Hecht |first=Hans |year=1997 |title=Cacti and Succulents |edition=p/b |location=New York |publisher=Sterling |isbn=978-0-8069-0549-5 |others=trans. A. Englander }}, p. 74</ref>
* ''Watering'' The Easter cactus is said to respond badly to over- or under-watering, e.g. by losing stem segments; continuously moist soil is recommended.<ref name=Brun2001/>
* ''Propagation'' Stem segments may be removed in late Spring and the cut surface allowed to dry out before being placed in slightly moist soil.<ref name=Hech1997/>
